newsitem.title: CANADA: Young incest victim granted asylum in Canada.
newsitem.headline: Young incest victim granted asylum in Canada.

text.p: Canada, in an unprecedented move, has granted a boy asylum on the grounds that Britain failed to protect him from sexual abuse by his father, authorities said on Thursday.

Officials said the decision, made in January and just recently published, marked the first time Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) considered a young victim of incest a member of "a particular social group" with a well-founded fear of persecution in his homeland.
It was also the first time an entire family was granted asylum in Canada based on a refugee claim by a child.

"In this case the panel found that the principal claimant, who was a 12-year-old boy at the time the claim was made (in 1995), was subjected to sexual abuse in Great Britain (and not protected)," said a source at the IRB, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
A spokesman for Canada's Citizenship and Immigration Department said the government was "reviewing all of our options" before deciding whether to appeal the board's decision.

The board heard that the boy, who holds dual British and U.S. citizenship, was sexually abused by his father and paternal grandparents in Britain until 1991. The boy, whose name was not disclosed, now lives in Toronto.

Evidence that the boy's mother sought assistance from various British authorities, but was rebuffed, led the board to rule that there was "clear and convincing proof that the U.K. failed to extend him adequate and effective protection."

The board concluded that the boy was denied basic rights guaranteed under the U.N. Convention on the Rights of the Child. Those include state protection from sexual abuse and separation from the offending parent.

The boy, who was born in the United States in 1984, moved to Britain as an infant with his parents, but returned to the United States with his mother and stepfather in 1992 on the advice of the U.S. embassy in London.
But in 1994 the boy's stepfather was deported to Britain after U.S. immigration learned that he had previous convictions for drug offences, although he had been pardoned for the offences in Britain.
The Canadian board ruled that because U.S. officials had not considered the rights of the boy in deporting his stepfather, the boy was also a victim of persecution in the United States.
The family moved to Canada after the stepfather's deportation and applied for refugee status.
